world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Beale, Tony. 1974. A grammar of the Biri language of north Queensland. AIATSIS ms; also Terrill, A. 1993. Biri (BA Hons thesis, ANU) and Holmer 1983 (named on Wikipedia 'Biri language'; none readable online).

new_statements.quote: 2.11 Word or syllable stress is not significant in any of the languages studied here. The spoken context runs smooth without emphasis of any syllable unless in cases of long vowels (or diphthongs), besides not very frequent in the Gunggari languages. As usual, in a spoken context or sequence of syllables, however, the second initial syllable often carries mechanically more stress than the others (cf. in Part I, 2.9), which explains the origin of such shortened forms as ḏe· (Gun EA) for jinḏia where?; this tendency is frequently reflected in the current pronunciation of place names of several syllables, derived from Aboriginal words, in Queensland: Barálba, Mundúbbera etc.
new_statements.citation: Holmer, Nils M. 1983. Linguistic survey of south-eastern Queensland. Pacific Linguistics D-54. Canberra: Australian National University. Part II, The languages of the Gunggari group, §2.11, p. 178 (with Part I §2.9, p. 5).
new_statements.locator: Part II §2.11, p. 178 (PDF page 186); supporting: Part I §2.9, p. 5 (PDF page 13); Birri chapter §21.1-21.2, p. 301 (PDF page 309)
new_statements.reading: no word stress according to the source
new_statements.rule_in_words: Per Holmer, word or syllable stress is not phonologically significant in Birri or any other Gunggari-group language; connected speech runs without emphasis on any syllable except long vowels/diphthongs, but in longer words and utterances the second syllable tends 'mechanically' to carry more stress than the others (Part I §2.9, p. 5: 'Stress is not significant in any of the languages dealt with in this survey. Still a certain tendency persists everywhere to stress the vowel of the second initial syllable in words or utterances of some length'). If one must assign a position, the source points to the second syllable (fixed-second would be the alternative reading), but the source's own claim is non-significance.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not stated for Birri. For Bidjara (same group, Part II §8.5, p. 205) Holmer adds 'secondary stress appearing on subsequent alternate syllables' after the second-syllable accent, e.g. bibanagana 'looking at a paper'.
new_statements.exceptions: Long vowels or diphthongs are the only case where a syllable is emphasised (and these are said to be infrequent in Gunggari languages); non-initial vowel length in Birri is 'occasional' and left unmarked (§21.2, p. 301). Part I §2.9 adds that the second-syllable tendency explains shortened forms (aphaeresis of initial syllables).
new_statements.domain_note: Holmer's statement is made once for all seven languages of his Gunggari group (Gunggari, Bidjara, Marganj, Gangulu, Wirri, Birri, Ngawun; abbreviation list on the same p. 178 includes 'Bir Birri'), and the Birri chapter (§21.1, p. 301) says Birri's phonetic structure 'does not in any important respect differ' from those languages. The domain is connected speech / 'words or utterances of some length' rather than citation forms; salvage data from a handful of last speakers (Nebo, Strathmore, Ukanunda/Bowen dialects, pp. 300-301).
new_statements.identity_note: Holmer 1983 treats 'Birri' (pp. 300-318; informants from Nebo, Strathmore/Bowen River, Ukanunda/Bowen, Mackay, Burdekin; called biri, birija, birijaba by speakers) and 'Wirri' (pp. 282-299; Clermont informants) as separate languages of his Gunggari group. Both fall under Glottolog biri1256 (Glottolog bib tags Wirri = Biri [bzr]). The stress statement (Part II §2.11, p. 178) is made for the whole Gunggari group (Gunggari, Bidjara, Marganj, Gangulu, Wirri, Birri, Ngawun), not for Birri alone; the Birri chapter explicitly assimilates Birri's phonetics to the group (§21.1, p. 301). Note also that Glottolog's listing of Thieberger 1996 (a Western Australian handbook) under biri1256 is a computerized misassignment.

The spoken context runs smooth without emphasis of any syllable unless in cases of long vowels (or diphthongs), besides not very frequent in the Gunggari languages. sources.locator: Part II §2.11, p. 178 (PDF page 186); supporting: Part I §2.9, p. 5 (PDF page 13); Birri chapter §21.1-21.2, p. 301 (PDF page 309)
sources.note: Part I 2.9 (p. 5) and Part II 2.11 (p. 178): stress is not significant/distinctive in any language of the survey; a mechanical tendency to give more stress to the 'second initial syllable' in longer words or utterances (cf. place names Baralba, Mundubbera). The Birri chapter's own phonology (21.1-21.5, pp. 301-302) says Birri's phonetic structure does not differ in any important respect from the other Gunggari languages, notes non-initial vowel length is occasional and left unmarked, and says nothing further about stress.
